# The menstrual cycle

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Pediatrics > Pediatric gynecology > The menstrual cycle*

[Original Article Link](/library/Ek08pT)

---

## Summary

The menstrual cycle is a highly regulated physiological process required for <u>conception</u> and <u>pregnancy</u>. From the start of <u>menstruation</u> (<u>menarche</u>) to its cessation (<u>menopause</u>), menstrual bleeding (<u>menstruation</u>) is regulated by the coordinated release of <u>hormones</u> from the <u>hypothalamus</u>, <u>pituitary gland</u>, and <u>ovaries</u>. These <u>hormones</u> trigger simultaneous changes in the <u>ovaries</u> (<u>ovarian cycle</u>) and the <u>uterus</u> (<u>uterine cycle</u>). <u>Mittelschmerz</u> is a physiological condition experienced by some individuals characterized by unilateral lower abdominal <u>pain</u> during <u>ovulation</u>; it may be initially misdiagnosed as <u>appendicitis</u>, <u>ectopic pregnancy</u>, or <u>ovarian torsion</u> in individuals who present with acute <u>pelvic pain</u> or <u>acute abdomen</u>. Management involves reassurance and <u>nonopioid analgesics</u>.




<u>Menstrual cycle abnormalities</u> include changes in the frequency and intensity of <u>menstruation</u> as well as symptoms such as pronounced abdominal discomfort, gastrointestinal issues, and psychiatric symptoms. <u>Amenorrhea</u>, <u>dysmenorrhea</u>, <u>abnormal uterine bleeding</u>, and <u>premenstrual disorders</u> are discussed separately.

---

## Overview of the menstrual cycle

### Menstrual cycle




* The menstrual cycle is a highly regulated physiological process in which the coordinated release of <u>hormones</u> from the <u>hypothalamus</u>, <u>pituitary gland</u>, and <u>ovaries</u> produces a mature <u>oocyte</u> and prepares the <u>endometrium</u> for <u>blastocyst implantation</u>.

* Average cycle duration: 28 days (24–38 days)

* First day of <u>menstruation</u>: day 1 of the cycle

* Average duration of <u>menstruation</u>: 5 days [[3]](/library/4pd3pI0)

* Average blood loss: 35–50 mL

* Simultaneous changes in the <u>ovaries</u> (<u>ovarian cycle</u>) and the <u>uterus</u> (<u>uterine cycle</u>)

* <u>Ovarian cycle</u>: 3 phases, regulated by <u>hormones</u> released from the <u>hypothalamus and pituitary gland</u>

* <u>Follicular phase</u>: production and maturation of a <u>dominant follicle</u>

* <u>Ovulation</u>: release of the <u>oocyte</u> from the <u>dominant follicle</u>

* <u>Luteal phase</u>: formation and degeneration of the <u>corpus luteum</u>

* <u>Uterine cycle</u>: 3 phases, regulated by <u>hormones</u> released from the <u>ovary</u> during the <u>ovarian cycle</u>

* <u>Menstrual phase</u>: <u>endometrial desquamation</u>

* <u>Proliferative phase</u>: <u>regeneration</u> of the <u>functional layer of the endometrium</u>

* <u>Secretory phase</u>: <u>endometrial</u> differentiation in preparation for possible <u>blastocyst implantation</u>

## Ovarian cycle

* Follicular phase (approx. day 1–14) ;   [[4]](/library/PpdWpI0)

* The <u>hypothalamus</u> releases <u>gonadotropin-releasing hormone</u> (<u>GnRH</u>) in pulses, stimulating the <u>anterior pituitary gland</u> to release <u>follicle-stimulating hormone</u> (<u>FSH</u>) and <u>luteinizing hormone</u> (<u>LH</u>).

* <u>FSH</u> and <u>LH</u> stimulate the growth of a cohort of antral follicles.

* <u>LH</u> stimulates ovarian <u>theca cells</u> and induces the production of <u>progesterone</u> and <u>androstenedione</u> (substrates for <u>estradiol</u> synthesis in <u>granulosa cells</u>).

* <u>FSH</u> stimulates ovarian <u>granulosa cells</u>, which produce <u>estradiol</u> and <u>inhibin</u>.

* <u>Estradiol</u> and <u>inhibin</u> block the release of <u>gonadotropins</u> (negative feedback).

* Decreasing <u>FSH</u> levels lead to a regression of all follicles except one <u>dominant follicle</u>, which continues to develop despite falling <u>FSH</u> levels.  [[5]](/library/UodbYI0)

* The <u>dominant follicle</u> produces high levels of <u>estradiol</u>, which leads to a switch from negative to positive feedback in the <u>hypothalamus and pituitary gland</u>, resulting in a rapid increase in <u>gonadotropin</u> levels (<u>LH surge</u>).  [[6]](/library/dodoaI0)

* Ovulation (approx. day 14): LH surge induces the release of the mature <u>oocyte</u> from the <u>dominant follicle</u>.

* Luteal phase (for 14 days after <u>ovulation</u>) ; : 

* The ruptured follicle transforms into the <u>corpus luteum</u>, primarily producing <u>progesterone</u> and some <u>estradiol</u>.

* <u>Progesterone</u> and <u>estradiol</u> inhibit <u>gonadotropin</u> release (switch back to negative feedback).

* In the absence of <u>fertilization</u>, falling <u>LH</u> levels lead to degeneration of the <u>corpus luteum</u>.

* Discontinuation of <u>progesterone</u> and <u>estradiol</u> production by the <u>corpus luteum</u> results in cessation of <u>gonadotropin</u> inhibition, initiating the <u>follicular phase</u>.

## Uterine cycle

* Menstrual phase (day 1 to approx. day 5)

* In the absence of <u>fertilization</u>, the <u>corpus luteum</u> degenerates.

* Decreasing <u>progesterone</u> and <u>estradiol</u> levels induce vasospasms and <u>ischemia</u> in the uterine <u>spiral arteries</u> and <u>apoptosis</u> of the <u>functional layer of the endometrium</u>.  [[7]](/library/IpdYII0)[[8]](/library/rpdfII0)[[9]](/library/7pd4II0)

* These changes lead to shedding of the <u>endometrial</u> lining, which manifests as <u>menstruation</u>.

* Proliferative phase of the menstrual cycle (approx. day 5–14): <u>Estradiol</u> produced by the growing follicles promotes <u>endometrial</u> <u>proliferation</u>.

* Uterine <u>spiral arteries</u> regenerate and extend two-thirds of the way into the <u>endometrium</u>.

* Stromal cells divide, enlarge, and accumulate <u>glycogen</u>.

* <u>Endometrial</u> glands become straight, tubular, and lined by simple <u>columnar epithelium</u>.

* <u>Endometrial</u> <u>epithelial</u> cells proliferate (cells have high <u>mitotic</u> activity).

* Secretory phase (approx. day 14–28): <u>Progesterone</u> from the <u>corpus luteum</u> promotes <u>endometrial</u> differentiation and other changes that prepare the body for <u>blastocyst implantation</u>.

* Stromal cells become <u>edematous</u> and uterine <u>spiral arteries</u> extend the full length of the <u>endometrium</u>.

* <u>Endometrial</u> glands increase <u>tortuosity</u> and production of <u>glycogen</u>-rich secretions.

* <u>Basal body temperature</u> increases.

* Cervical mucus secretion increases, which protects the <u>uterus</u> from foreign substances and cells (e.g., <u>sperm</u>).

---

## Physiological age-related changes in the menstrual cycle

* First few years after <u>menarche</u>: irregular menstrual cycles (due to immaturity of the <u>hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis</u>)

* 25–30 years of age: Menstrual cycles are longest.

* <u>Perimenopause</u>: irregular menstrual cycles (due to fluctuating <u>hormone</u> levels)

---

## Mittelschmerz

<u>Mittelschmerz</u> (also known as <u>midcycle pain</u> or <u>ovulatory pain</u>) is physiological <u>pain</u> experienced by some individuals during <u>ovulation</u>. [[10]](/library/rldfyJ0)[[11]](/library/9mdN3q0)




### <u>Epidemiology</u>




<u>Mittelschmerz</u> occurs at least once in > 50% of <u>premenopausal</u> individuals. [[12]](/library/YIdnYr0)




### Etiology [[12]](/library/YIdnYr0)




* Unclear

* Proposed etiologies include:

* Enlargement and rupture of the <u>follicular cyst</u>

* Spasms of the <u>fallopian tubes</u> or <u>uterus</u>

* Transient <u>peritoneal</u> irritation from follicular fluid or blood





### Clinical features




* Unilateral lower abdominal <u>pain</u> (often recurrent) [[12]](/library/YIdnYr0)[[13]](/library/7ld4yJ0)

* <u>Pain</u> occurs mid-cycle (days 14–16 of the menstrual cycle) in individuals with regular cycles.

* Usually located in the iliac fossa but may be generalized [[13]](/library/7ld4yJ0)[[14]](/library/RSdlz60)

* Can last from minutes up to 48 hours [[10]](/library/rldfyJ0)[[14]](/library/RSdlz60)

* May be accompanied by ovulation bleeding: light bleeding or blood-stained discharge during the midpoint of the menstrual cycle [[15]](/library/OmdIfq0)

* <u>Physical examination</u>

* Lower abdominal <u>pain</u> on palpation [[16]](/library/Cmdq3q0)

* Possible <u>referred pain</u> and <u>rebound tenderness</u> [[16]](/library/Cmdq3q0)

* Adnexal tenderness or, rarely, a mass [[14]](/library/RSdlz60)[[17]](/library/omd0gq0)





### Diagnostics




* <u>Clinical diagnosis</u> [[11]](/library/9mdN3q0)[[12]](/library/YIdnYr0)

* If there is diagnostic uncertainty, consider <u>laboratory studies</u> or imaging to rule out <u>differential diagnoses of acute abdomen</u>.  [[12]](/library/YIdnYr0)[[16]](/library/Cmdq3q0)

* <u>Pelvic</u> <u>ultrasound</u> (if performed) may show signs of <u>ovulation</u>, e.g.: [[18]](/library/LmdwTq0)

* A small amount of <u>intraperitoneal</u> fluid

* <u>Increased echogenicity</u> in <u>ovarian follicles</u>





> [!WARNING]
> It may be difficult to distinguish between symptoms of <u>mittelschmerz</u> and those of <u>acute appendicitis</u> or other adnexal emergencies. [[12]](/library/YIdnYr0)[[16]](/library/Cmdq3q0)




### Management




* Reassurance and ; <u>nonopioid analgesics</u> (e.g., <u>NSAIDs</u>) as needed [[11]](/library/9mdN3q0)[[13]](/library/7ld4yJ0)

* For recurrent episodes, consider <u>hormonal contraception</u> to suppress <u>ovulation</u>. [[19]](/library/7md4Sq0)

## Abnormalities of the menstrual cycle

Abnormal menstrual patterns include changes in the frequency, intensity, and/or onset of bleeding. Common manifestations of <u>menstrual cycle abnormalities</u> include:




* <u>Dysmenorrhea</u> (painful <u>menstruation</u>)

* <u>Amenorrhea</u> (absence of <u>menstruation</u>)

* <u>Abnormal uterine bleeding</u> (e.g., increased frequency and/or volume of <u>menstruation</u>)

* <u>Premenstrual disorders</u> (cyclical physical, psychological, and behavioral changes before <u>menstruation</u>)

* Anovulatory cycle: The menstrual cycle may be irregular in <u>adolescents</u> during the first few months/years after <u>menarche</u>.
* Immaturity of the <u>hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis</u> → irregular secretion of <u>gonadotropins</u> → short <u>luteal phase</u>, and lack of <u>progesterone</u> → <u>endometrium</u> remains in the <u>proliferative phase</u> → irregular <u>menses</u> and <u>heavy menstrual bleeding</u>
* Does not require treatment because <u>menses</u> become regular as <u>hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis</u> matures
